name: Basic of Vaccine
blurb: USMLE vaccine platforms, immunology, mechanisms, contraindications and examples

topics.name: Vaccine basics
topics.desc: Integrated high-yield Anki cards; not a clinical immunization schedule

cards.q: Vaccination vs passive immunization: what is the distinction?
cards.a: Vaccination induces active immunity: host B/T-cell response and memory, with delayed onset. Passive immunity supplies ready-made antibodies: immediate, temporary protection, no memory.

cards.q: Live attenuated vaccines: mechanism, immune response, pros/cons?
cards.a: Weakened living organism replicates transiently → strong humoral + cellular immunity, often durable. Risks: disease in severely immunocompromised hosts; rare reversion for some vaccines.

cards.q: Live vaccines: examples and contraindications?
cards.a: MMR, varicella, rotavirus, BCG, yellow fever, intranasal flu, oral polio (Sabin), oral Ty21a typhoid, smallpox; oral adenovirus in military. Avoid in pregnancy and severe immunodeficiency.

cards.q: HIV and live vaccines: what is the nuance?
cards.a: Some live vaccines (e.g., MMR, varicella) may be used in selected patients with HIV and adequate immune function (often CD4 ≥200 cells/µL in adults); assess vaccine-specific guidance.

cards.q: Killed/inactivated vaccines: mechanism, response, advantages/limitations?
cards.a: Whole pathogen inactivated by heat/chemicals; retains epitopes but cannot replicate. Mainly antibody response; safer than live, usually less cellular immunity and needs boosters/adjuvants.

cards.q: Killed/inactivated: classic examples and formulation traps?
cards.a: Hepatitis A, rabies, inactivated IM influenza, inactivated polio (Salk/IPV). Typhoid Vi is a purified polysaccharide, NOT whole-killed. Oral Ty21a typhoid is live.

cards.q: Subunit vaccine: definition, response, examples?
cards.a: Contains selected pathogen antigens, not whole organism. Often mainly humoral response, sometimes needs adjuvant/boosters. Examples: acellular pertussis; HepB and HPV are recombinant subunits.

cards.q: Recombinant protein vaccine: what makes it 'recombinant'?
cards.a: Antigen is manufactured by genetically engineered cells; 'recombinant' describes production, not a unique immune mechanism. Examples: HepB HBsAg, HPV L1 VLPs, zoster glycoprotein E.

cards.q: Pure polysaccharide vaccine: mechanism, immune response, age limitation?
cards.a: Unconjugated capsular sugar cross-links B-cell receptors → T-independent (TI-2), mainly IgM, limited class switching/memory; weak in children <2 yr. Example: PPSV23.

cards.q: Conjugate vaccine: how does it create T-cell help?
cards.a: Capsular polysaccharide linked to carrier protein. Sugar-specific B cell internalizes it, presents carrier peptides on MHC II → CD4 T-cell help → IgG switching, affinity maturation, memory.

cards.q: Pure polysaccharide vs conjugate: compare high-yield outcomes.
cards.a: PPSV23: sugar alone, T-independent, weak memory, poor <2 yr. PCV/Hib/MenACWY conjugates: sugar+protein, T-dependent, strong memory, effective in infants.

cards.q: What do subunit, recombinant, polysaccharide and conjugate each describe?
cards.a: Subunit = only part of pathogen. Recombinant = how antigen is made. Polysaccharide = sugar antigen. Conjugate = sugar chemically linked to protein. Categories overlap.

cards.q: Which vaccine examples belong to which subunit family?
cards.a: HepB = recombinant HBsAg; HPV = recombinant L1 VLP; aP = purified pertussis proteins; PPSV23 = pure polysaccharide; PCV/Hib/MenACWY = conjugates; Shingrix = recombinant gE + adjuvant.

cards.q: Toxoid vaccines: what is injected, what is protected against?
cards.a: Inactivated bacterial exotoxin retains antigenicity without toxicity → neutralizing antitoxin antibodies. Examples: tetanus and diphtheria. Antibody titers wane → boosters.

cards.q: Toxoid vs conjugate: what role does protein play?
cards.a: Toxoid: detoxified toxin itself is target of protective antibodies. Conjugate: carrier protein recruits helper T cells to improve response against linked capsular sugar.

cards.q: mRNA vaccines: mechanism and immune response?
cards.a: Lipid nanoparticles deliver mRNA into cytoplasm → ribosomes make antigen → humoral + cellular responses. mRNA does not need to enter nucleus or alter DNA.

cards.q: mRNA vaccines: advantages, adverse effects and example?
cards.a: Rapid design; no live pathogen; can be used in pregnancy when indicated. Local pain, fatigue, headache, myalgia; rare myocarditis/pericarditis (especially young males). Example: SARS-CoV-2.

cards.q: Live vs inactivated influenza and polio: distinguish routes.
cards.a: Influenza: live attenuated intranasal vs inactivated IM. Polio: live oral Sabin (OPV) vs inactivated injectable Salk (IPV). Route and formulation change contraindications.

cards.q: Why do protein conjugates work well in infants <2 years?
cards.a: Infants respond poorly to TI-2 capsular polysaccharides. Carrier peptides activate CD4 helper T cells → germinal centers, class switching and memory.

cards.q: Asplenia: which pathogens/vaccines are especially important?
cards.a: Encapsulated bacteria: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae type b. Review pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib vaccines.

cards.q: Pregnancy: live vs non-live vaccine principle?
cards.a: Live MMR/varicella contraindicated. Inactivated influenza and Tdap are recommended when indicated; mRNA COVID-19 vaccines can be used under current recommendations.

cards.q: Humoral vs cellular immunity: which vaccine platforms tend to induce each?
cards.a: Live attenuated and mRNA can elicit both B- and T-cell responses. Killed, toxoid and conventional protein subunits mainly stimulate antibody responses; adjuvants alter response.

cards.q: What is an adjuvant and why is it used?
cards.a: An added immune stimulant that enhances antigen presentation/innate signaling and antibody responses; particularly useful with inactivated or subunit vaccines.

cards.q: What is a virus-like particle (VLP)?
cards.a: Self-assembled viral structural proteins without viral genome; noninfectious but display repetitive antigens. Example: recombinant HPV L1 vaccines.

cards.q: What are the two classic vaccine USMLE traps?
cards.a: 1) PPSV23 (T-independent) vs PCV (T-dependent). 2) OPV live vs IPV killed; intranasal flu live vs IM flu inactivated.
